newsitem.title: FRANCE: Votes show Eurosceptics on rise across continent.
newsitem.headline: Votes show Eurosceptics on rise across continent.

text.p: From Austria's Alpine pastures to a mining town on the edge of the French city of Marseille, voters delivered a nationalist, Eurosceptical protest message on Sunday which governments ignore at their peril.

In Austria, the anti-Maastricht Freedom Party of hard-right leader Joerg Haider surged to 28 percent of the vote in the first European Parliament elections since the country joined the European Union last year.

In France, anti-Maastricht Communist and extreme-right National Front candidates shared a record 64 percent of the vote in a parliamentary by-election regarded as a national test, and will face each other in a run-off next Sunday.

In both countries, voters used elections where national power was not at stake to register anger at austerity policies which they blame, rightly or wrongly, on the drive for a single European currency launched by the Maastricht Treaty in 1991.

"This was an expression of anger at government policy conducted in the name of Europe," French political commentator Philippe Alexandre said of the by-election in Gardanne, near Marseille, where more than 60 percent of voters abstained.
The Austrian vote bolstered the Freedom Party's standing as the most popular far-right party in Europe, ahead of its French sister party led by anti-immigration crusader Jean-Marie Le Pen.

Haider, best known abroad for having praised Adolf Hitler's employment policies, told reporters: "We are against Maastricht and we will join with all members of the European Parliament who think the same way...We want a Europe of the fatherlands, one that gives power to the people."

While domestic politics played a major role in both votes, the results reflected a nationalist backlash among voters in many EU countries, visible in votes in Denmark, Belgium and Sweden and in the ructions among Britain's ruling Conservatives.

They highlight a growing gulf between governments of all mainstream parties which are adopting tight austerity budgets in the race to meet the criteria for European monetary union in 1999, and public opinion which increasingly blames the pain of unemployment, welfare cutbacks and high taxes on Europe.

New EU member Finland's Social Democratic-led government put its faith in Europe at the weekend by bringing its currency into the European Monetary System's exchange-rate mechanism, a prelude to joining the single currency.
Finnish voters may give their verdict next weekend when they elect their European Parliament members for the first time.

A rare exception to the trend may be Germany, where the opposition Social Democrats were drubbed in regional elections in March when they adopted a Eurosceptical message, demanding a postponement of the single currency.
But even there, Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Bavarian sister party is sounding increasingly Eurosceptical while Bonn demands a cut in its EU budget contribution with growing stridency.
Governments differ on the lessons they should draw from the backlash in the current negotiations on reforming the EU.

While Britain argues that voters do not want any further EU integration or transfer of national sovereignty, France and Germany say the public wants a more effective and integrated Europe on issues such as law and order, drugs and immigration as well as in foreign and defence policy.

On one point, however, the Austrian vote may unite EU member states: few if any will be keen to increase the powers of a European Parliament where a growing number of mavericks and extremists elected in protest votes are joining second-rank politicians often exiled to the Strasbourg-based assembly.
